extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and public administration; practitioners interested in theory of politics-administration relations
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative and analytical criteria about the proper relation between politics (expression of the state will) and administration (execution), including limits of political control, independence of authorities, and central vs local administration tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between constitution-making and legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitution-making often requires action of a special governmental organ (constitutional convention) and of the people as a whole, whereas legislation may be enacted by the legislative body alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a special, broader participatory process for constitutional change; ordinary legislative processes suffice for ordinary legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organs that judge constitutional compliance become political organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Where organs (e.g., courts) determine in concrete cases whether legislative acts comply with the constitution, they become constitutional, and therefore political, organs that aid in expressing the will of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize judicial review as part of the political function insofar as it shapes the state's expressed will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary and secondary functions of politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics has primarily to do with the expression of the will of the state and secondarily with its execution; harmony between expression (making law) and execution (enforcing law) is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political arrangements by how well they secure harmony between lawmaking and law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of political control over administration (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body which expresses the state will must have some control over the body which executes it in order to secure execution and harmonious government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide political oversight sufficient to ensure execution, but avoid overreach (see limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible loci of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of administration may be found either inside the formal governmental system or outside it (e.g., political parties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing control mechanisms, consider both formal institutional checks and extra-governmental political structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control must be limited to what is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Political control should extend only so far as is necessary to produce harmony between expression and execution of the state will; if extended beyond that limit, it loses its raison d'être.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expanding political control for partisan perpetuation or extraneous aims; restrict control to functions necessary for faithful execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of using control to perpetuate party organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Control extended beyond necessary limits can be used to perpetuate a particular party organization instead of ensuring that the expressed state will becomes an actual rule of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against using administrative control for party entrenchment or to suppress spontaneous popular expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that excessive political control prevents popular expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper exercise of control may prevent spontaneous expression by the people of the popular will, introducing artificial elements into the expression of the state will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate controls by their effects on popular responsiveness and genuine public expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive control harms administrative efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: If control is extended too far, administration is discharged with reference to influencing future state will rather than executing an already expressed will, thereby hampering efficient administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should ensure administrators can focus on execution rather than political engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political bodies' tendency to improperly influence administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies that express the state will are always tempted to use their powers of control to influence future expressions of the state will, whether from patriotic or selfish motives, resulting in partial administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutional safeguards to reduce incentives and opportunities for such influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial administration as crucial safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial and interested administration of the law produces grave evils; many progressive societies have moved to secure independence for certain authorities entrusted with administering the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote institutional independence (especially judicial) to protect impartial administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of concurrence by independent authority (English model)
rubrics_metrics.description: In England the principle that no rule of conduct should be enforced until concurrence of some authority independent of the authority laying down the rule is often required; this underlies judicial and administrative independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require independent checks (e.g., an independent judiciary or executing body concurrence) before enforcement of state directives where impartiality is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special need for impartial administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration of justice must be executed impartially, with as little regard as possible to the effect a particular decision will have upon future expressions of the state will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insulate judicial decision-making from political pressures that aim to shape future policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence as political norm (Anglo-American)
rubrics_metrics.description: English-speaking peoples have generally accepted that the danger of permitting political bodies to control the administration of justice is so great that judicial authorities should have very great independence, even at risk of depriving the expressed will of being an actual rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept some tension between democratic control and judicial independence as a tradeoff for impartial justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of local administrative authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The English rule of requiring concurrence of an independent authority was applied beyond courts to administration and most prominently in the system of local government, giving local administrative authorities significant independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider granting local administrators sufficient autonomy to prevent central political manipulation of enforcement in areas where impartiality and local discretion matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap between legal independence and political practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States administrative bodies have legal independence vis-à-vis legislatures but in practice have been subjected to control by political parties, decreasing administrative efficiency and causing divergence between formal law and real state will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish formal legal design from political realities; adopt measures to reduce party capture of administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration should have some political control to encourage initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike courts, administrative authorities should be subjected to political control so that they take active initiative in executing the law; courts merely execute the law on application of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance independence with responsiveness: administrators need direction to act pro-actively within public policy aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting administration from undue political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The undue extension of politics over administration can be prevented by recognizing a degree of independence in administrative authorities and cultivating sound public opinion as protection against partisan influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine institutional safeguards (legal independence) with civic safeguards (public opinion, norms) to protect administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics encompasses multiple functions and actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics embraces constitution-making, legislation, selection of governmental officers, and control of execution; no single governmental authority can alone discharge this complex function—multiple organs (convention, courts, legislature, executive, local authorities, parties) share it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design political-institutional systems that allocate these functions among complementary actors while managing overlaps and conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal/fractional nature of states and local needs
rubrics_metrics.description: All states are composed of local communities with needs separate from the state; states must be divided into districts for matters of state concern, and local communities often function as administrative districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional arrangements should account for local distinctiveness when assigning administrative and legislative responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict over spheres of state vs local competence
rubrics_metrics.description: If matters of competence between state and local spheres conflict, final decision by either state supremacy or local supremacy yields either centralization or state disintegration respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constitutional, judicial, and political mechanisms to mediate conflicts and avoid extremes of excessive centralization or fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of constitutional delimitation handled by courts and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A written constitution may attempt to delimit state and local spheres, but courts interpreting it are influenced by origin and political thought; public opinion often helps prevent too great centralization or disintegration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on a mix of legal rules and civic norms; anticipate that judicial interpretation will reflect political context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative arrangements can make theory and practice diverge
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if theory assigns expression to central organs and execution to the state, if actual execution is given to local communities free from effective state control, the local will may modify the state's expressed will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay careful attention to who actually executes policy; formal assignment of powers may be undermined by execution arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and tradeoffs of local self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: Local self-government often pairs centralized legislation with decentralized administration, enabling local communities to modify or not enforce unpopular state laws; this preserves local expression but may undermine uniform state enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits of local responsiveness against costs to uniformity and state-wide objectives; use state supervisory mechanisms when necessary (example: NY State Board of Health enforcing public health law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and tradeoffs of administrative centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative centralization reserves execution to centrally appointed and controlled officials (e.g., prefects), often executing policies recognized as local by law; it preserves state unity but sacrifices local autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When centralizing, ensure mechanisms for local input or compensatory local expression to avoid alienation and loss of local interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neither pure centralization nor pure local self-government is ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Local self-government tends to obstruct state interests by hindering execution where state unity is needed; administrative centralization tends to sacrifice local interests by insufficiently providing for local execution. Neither produces harmonious state-local relations by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for a balanced regime that differentiates spheres and combines central oversight with local discretion where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamics: historical moves toward centralization or decentralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Political systems have tended to shift—England and U.S. toward centralization of administration; France and Germany moving toward greater local autonomy for expression and execution—reflecting attempts to balance competing needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy reforms should be context-sensitive and responsive to administrative complexity and demands for local expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of constitutional prohibitions on special legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions in constitutions against special legislation to secure local autonomy have been ineffective because (1) localities cannot be fully removed from state control without risking disintegration, and (2) legislatures often evade these prohibitions through fine-grained classification (practical special legislation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional protections with realistic enforcement mechanisms; anticipate legislative workarounds and judicial accommodations for local development needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial deference to legislative classifications for local development
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have often upheld minute classifications and departures from formal general acts on grounds that without such legislative flexibility local development is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize judicial balancing between formal prohibitions and practical needs; reforms seeking local autonomy must address both legal form and political incentives.
